text: It started in the dark. Whistles. Bugles. Shepherd's horns. Then shapes moving across the snow. At Yudam-ni the Fifth and Seventh Marines had settled in around the village. They held the surrounding ridges in a rough ring. That night two Chinese divisions came for them and a third moved to cut the road behind them. The attackers came in waves. They hit the hills the Marines knew by their map numbers. Hill twelve-eighty-two. Hill twelve-forty. Hill fourteen-oh-three. Grenades bounced down the slopes. Machine guns fired until their barrels glowed. Marines fought from foxholes they had barely scraped into the frozen ground. Company after company was cut to pieces. Some positions held. Some were overrun and then retaken before dawn. On Hill twelve-eighty-two one Marine company was reduced to a handful of men. Cooks and clerks and drivers grabbed rifles and climbed the hill to fill the gaps. By morning the snow around Yudam-ni was dark with fallen soldiers. The Marines had held. But they soon learned the true scale of the attack. The Chinese had not only struck at Yudam-ni. They had struck everywhere at once. The road south to Hagaru-ri was cut. At Toktong Pass halfway down a single rifle company was surrounded on a lonely hill. At Hagaru-ri itself enemy troops stormed toward the half-finished airstrip. East of the reservoir the Army regiment known as Task Force Faith was fighting for its life. The Ninth Army Group had done exactly what Mao wanted. It had cut the First Marine Division into isolated pockets. Each one surrounded. Each one alone. In Tokyo the mood shifted from confidence to shock. MacArthur sent word to Washington that his forces now faced an entirely new war. On November twenty-ninth a relief column of British Royal Marine commandos and American troops fought north from Koto-ri. The Chinese ambushed it in a narrow valley. Trucks burned. The column was split apart. Survivors would call that stretch of road Hell Fire Valley. Only part of the force broke through. For the men at Yudam-ni the situation was now clear. They were fourteen miles from Hagaru-ri. Every mile of that road was controlled by the enemy. And they had hundreds of wounded who could not walk. So what happens to an army when every road is closed and the enemy surrounds it on all sides? Before we answer that question here is a quick request.
